This is a really good question.

To answer the question in the title, it doesn't take much to change the gravity. One of the methods we use to find oil is by measuring the strength of gravity over an oil field. We don't really do this much anymore, but the same technology is being used to find where people tunnel across borders. So if you were going to remove enough soil and rock to make a tunnel, that would be enough that we could sense the difference in gravity using machines.

To change the gravity to a point where we would notice without machines is a bit trickier. Lets say you remove a mountain from earths mass. In theory this would change your weight by a noticeable amount (a pound or two). In practice it depends on the shape of what you removed, where you removed it from, and where you placed it. If you move the mountain to the other side of the world, then all you have done is shifted the earths center of gravity a little bit. You weight the same. If you place it in orbit around Earth then the tidal forces of this mountain will either make you weigh more or less (this isn't exactly right, you'll weigh less total, but how much depends on the following), depending on where you stand in relation to the mountain in it's orbit. If it is on the same side as you, you will weigh less because the mountain's gravity is acting against earths gravity, and if you are opposite the mountain then you will weigh more since both gravities (sp?) work together.

If you totally remove the mountain from earth's gravity well, then you will weigh less.

To answer the other questions I find it useful to think of rock as a slow moving fluid, and earth as a boiling sphere. What replaces the rock is going to depend on where it was removed from. At the surface of the earth rock is brittle. Towards the center it is liquid. What about in between? Rock is a really good insulator, so it traps heat in and keeps cold out. Because of this the rock deeper down wants to melt. On the other hand though, rock is heavy, and all that weight is pushing down on the rock, holding the atoms that are heating up and wanting to move in place. What happens in this case is that the rock acts like silly putty. It is a solid that flows. For the sake of simplicity, this is the mantle. When something is removed from on top of the mantle, the pressure that was keeping it semi-solid is reduced, and the rock starts to act more liquid. Since the pressure is still squeezing from below and the sides this pushes the mantle up. If enough pressure is reduced quickly enough then the mantle rock turns from plastic to liquid, and it will rush towards the surface where it either erupts as a volcano, or becomes an underground magma chamber. Of course gravity still plays a roll, and things will fall down, but the deeper you go, the more stuff comes up relative to whats falling down.

Earthquakes will almost definitely happen. If just fracturing aquifer rock will cause earthquakes then removing rock definitely will.

I think the worst thing that would happen if we started getting rid of earths mass is that we would go tectonically dead. The system would start to lose heat (since rock is a good insulator), and the mantle convection would slow, and then stop. This would show up as a reduction in tectonic earthquakes (the removal of rock would still cause earthquakes). As the mantle stopped, the outer core would stop convecting, and earth would lose it's magnetic field. Earth would lose its atmosphere, and we'd probably end up as a small red planet with no atmosphere and no water.

I would imagine that you would need some way of keeping them from floating away from each other. As far as gravity? With only the mass of a few coins at any given point, it would be almost imperceptible.

If we assume a primary and secondary mass of 0.1Kg and a radius of say 2 inches, the amount of force that would be exerted by the coins at any given point along the stack would be approximately 5.84X10-11lbf, or 258.6 piconewtons. This is of course a very rough estimate, but as you can see the gravity at the surface of the coins would be extremely low. Much, much lower than that of the earth, so any interaction between the coins bumping into one another, or other outside forces, would cause them to float apart very easily.
